ipc-title__text: I wanted a movie, and I didn't see one
ipc-html-content-inner-div:
Sheesh!  I really don't understand the reception this movie has gotten.  It was too long, and STILL it couldn't make me care about the characters. There were WAY too many LOUD fight scenes, and not enough plot and character development.  So many peaceful scenes were cut short by abrupt cuts to obnoxiously noisy following scenes, that I got sick of noticing how many times it happened.  How can a movie make you think about larger themes of good, evil and power when it doesn't give you *time* to think? 
And how are you supposed to care about the death of a character when there's hardly anything in the script about him up to that point?  How are you supposed to care about these different races when you know nothing about them?  We learn a little bit about hobbits, but not enough.  We learn hardly *anything*, zip, zero, about the race of men.  Ditto elves.  Why should we care about the romance of Arwen and Aragorn if we only get 1 tiny little scene about it?  (It amazes me that people say this movie has romance).  I cared somewhat about Frodo, but I got to the point where, if I saw him gazing at someone wide-eyed ONCE more I was going to stab myself through the head with my popcorn (this isn't as easy as it sounds).The special effects were great, but special effects, action scenes and wide-eyed gazing do NOT make a movie!

ipc-title__text: Not The Great Film That Folks Make It Out To Be
ipc-html-content-inner-div: "Lord of The Rings" is an enjoyable film, but it's not the great film that folks make it out to be. For the most part, the film is way too long and, at times, it's drawn out. The special effects are a bit too much.What makes the film watchable is the beautiful photography, and the solid performances from a first rate cast. This is the first film of a trilogy, and I suspect that the best is yet to come.

I can't remember a time where I have been compelled to see a movie in the cinema twice. The first time I saw it, I was blown away. The second time, I could sit back and enjoy it completely. Some of the highlights (not in order)-1. The transformation of Frodo from carefree hobbit, to someone with the weight of the world on his shoulders.  Elijah Wood was fantastic.  You could see the change in his eyes.2. Gandalf- Sir Ian McKellan, need I say more?3. Bilbo- I had tears in my eyes in every scene he was in.4. The fellowship mourning the death of Gandalf- It was understated but extremely moving.5. Enhancing some of the female characters- Yes, the purists will hate it, but reading the book as a young girl, it was hard not to feel a bit 'left out' of the adventure.6. Legolas- a magnificent presence (but I felt that more information could have been given about his background and motivation for joining the fellowship)7. Cinematography, costumes, cgi, script, direction- the attention to detail was amazing(hand-crafting of weaponry, New Zealand scenery), and there was a sense that the director nurtured and appreciated the actors' craft (as opposed to George Lucas, for example).8. The quality of acting in general- I was so happy that no big Hollywood 'names' were used.  It would have detracted from the ensemble nature of the characters.9. The score- subtle, happily lacking the bombastic 'John Williams' touch.
When I first heard that Peter Jackson had taken on the Tolkien trilogy, I was both scared and excited.  Scared, because it was such a momentous task, and excited because I truly believe that he is one of the few directors who could accomplish it.  I have seen and enjoyed all his films to date, and I believe that he is one of the most talented directors currently working. His achievement sends a strong message to struggling and aspiring directors, that you don't need to be a Hollywood yes-man to succeed.  If the Oscars have any integrity left, this film and the people who worked on it, should be strong contenders.  I would love to know how he persuaded NewLine to stake their future on these films.  It would make a great book, or maybe they could include it on the DVD :-)

I really liked this movie and I have read the books several times and some changes or omissions annoyed me but overall I am very pleased.A lot of people are under the mistaken idea that the Lord of the Rings is a trilogy, it isn't. Tolkien originally wrote it as a single book but the publishers forced him to divide it into three parts. Because of this there are no midway endings, the story just continues so the fact that the first film ends abruptly is unavoidable, unless you film the entire book or start doing really radical changes. So "Fellowship" is not the first part in a trilogy but rather the first part of one book.My final comment is that for those, like myself, who were bothered by some of the changes, try a second viewing were you can judge the film by itself and not compare it to the book.

ipc-title__text: Tedious, highly overrated, film is too long...

After that, I became annoyed by the violence and action sequences which just seemed to multiply with each step of the characters' journey and then slow the film's pace down. As an enthusiastic movie fan, I'm not sure what I expected...but unfortunately my expectations were too high based on all the hype this film has had for a year prior to its opening! Don't get me wrong, the actors were cast well, and they were quite wonderful and talented. Ditto on special effects and locations--the money spent does show up on the screen! However, I once heard it said that Speilberg likes to ask what an audience is "FEELING" in every scene, feeling on every page of a screenplay, because  when it comes right down to it film is about feeling and emotions. How you felt when you saw a movie is what you remember, what you see or hear is only temporary. It will be interesting to see how LOTR stands the test of time. In JAWS I jumped in my seat, and to this day two notes from the film's music and I feel danger lurking even when not near water! In E.T. I  felt like I helped lift that bike off the ground and saved E.T. In Wizard of Oz I feel hatred for that nasty witch, scared when the monkeys attacked, and triumph when the witch melts! What did I feel watching LOTR? That it was too long. That it was one foe-monster after another getting in the hero's way. That the quest was nothing more than one battle after another against each villain. That it was predictable even if you hadn't read the book. That the storyline was at fault for not having characters I truly cared about. That I felt cheated out of my ticket price because the ending proved the whole film was nothing but a set up for film two and three. I expected to care. I wanted to care. I didn't care. Well, in LOTR, I only felt disappointed. I felt no terror. I felt no joy. I felt no rage. I felt nothing except that I had watched a good movie, not a great movie! Although a classic series of books, I think this lack of  "feeling" is why this film is a hit for the computer/game crowd, but comes across as not that great to others. The week I saw LOTR I also saw to two other movies. VANILLA SKY and KATE & LEOPOLD. Now, here' s an interesting observation--- the only  film of the three that the audience applauded when it was over was KATE & LEOPOLD---because it made them FEEL GOOD, HAPPY, and glad they had lived the moments on screen along with Meg Ryan and Hugh Jackman.

The direction is ok but there are too many close up shot that leave you in a daze when you see one of the few action scenes. he does show off the landscape, which i admit does deserve oscars for production design. but the action is edited fast,bably and it becomes confusing. the set pieces are few and far between and your attention does wander through most of the film while you wait for something exiting to happen. I am not a moaner, i have enjoyed long films like GOODFELLAS, EYES WIDE SHUT, CASINO even GLADIATOR was better than this. don´t waste your time or money with this. to recover i sat through ARMY OF DARKNESS and SPARTACUS. films that kept my attention span and entertained me as well. sorry but when the hype dies you will know i speak the truth, you just may be too ashamed to admit it.

It is not an easy task to review this movie, as it was not an easy task to make it. Judging from the book, it might even be impossible.Honestly, when looking at Peter Jackson's work, if you haven't read the book, you can't help but think it's a really good heroic fantasy movie.But if you have... Well, maybe you were a little boy like Jackson when you read it, and you liked it for its cool fights and monsters. Yeah. Or maybe you were a grown-up who liked all these little details that set LOTR apart from the rest. And, frankly, when Jackson said he had to drop some of the best elements of the book (Tom Bombadil for example) because Tolkien's works were too rich to be adapted in their entirety, he forgot to tell us that he would use this extra time to add even more fight scenes, an orc-goblin hybrid (I don't remember this ? Not that it is of any interest...) and some stupid jokes.Really. What's with all the time the characters spent in the mines ? Sure, that looks good and impressive. But how about the *characters* themselves ? How about developing Samwise ? He's supposed to be fond of elves in the book. It isn't even mentioned once in the movie. Merry and Pippin ? Why are they so immature here ? Basically everyone was forgotten. Even Bilbo. He's supposed to be a joyful man, his bitterness shouldn't be visible, and as much as I like Ian Holm as an actor (although he seems to be doomed with characters which are as boring on film as they are fascinating on paper -- see From Hell), Jackson's Bilbo is not the Bilbo we know. Actually no one is the character we know. There are some good scenes, some characters are actually nicely depicted (Galadriel comes to mind), but that's all.Just a beautiful piece of a movie, with no soul at all. We want our mushrooms !

ipc-title__text: Sailing on the crest of literary reputation
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Being someone who has not read the books, I approached this movie as it should be approached; I had no expectations, no knowledge of the plot and no idea how it would be conveyed.I have read many reviews, all of which claim that The Fellowship of the Ring is an outstanding piece of cinema. That is undeniable.As a piece of cinema, it was as good as anything that has ever preceded it, however, a good movie, is not about cinema alone, there are so many more elements that are needed, such as narrative, dialogue, acting and pace.As superb as the cinematography and SFX were, I cannot help but feel that the other, more key, elements were indeed neglected.The opening narration from Cate Blanchett was probably the high point of the feature; I felt the excitement and the anticipation built here were wasted on such a poor movie.The dialogue was laughable, even cringe-worthy, how they got away with scripting that is unbelievable.The acting in general was poor, but this may have been a result of such a poor script, however, I feel compelled to exclude Ian McKellen, as he seemed to be the only cast member who put any feeling into their role.Throughout the three hours I noticed that, like most fantasy films, it was all a bit repetitive. How many times could they get into trouble, Frodo put on the ring and then escape, without it becoming monotonous?In all I am amazed at the amount of people who have contributed to this movie being currently (10th January 02) ranked #1 in the top 250 movies, over 21,000 people giving it a score of 10/10, maybe I was watching a different film.

ipc-title__text: A little long with little character development
ipc-html-content-inner-div: For the most part, I was disappointed in this movie.  Being a trilogy, I thought the characters should have been developed more and their personalities explored more since some of them will probably be in the next two movies which have already been made.  The story seems to meander with battle scene after battle scene, with unbelievable odds, reminisent of Rambo movies.  The movie could had been an hour shorter by cutting out a battle scene, or two.  There are just so many ways to destroy creatures.  I doubt that I would care to watch either of the next two sequels/books.  I can't understand the hype for this movie, at best it is average.

I saw the film. Surely it was not bad , but I personally don't believe that it was the legendary film, we were all waiting for.Reminded me of Indiana Jones. I will not, see it on dvd for sure. Too much advertisement for just a good film...

First, I'll start off by saying that I haven't read the books.  However, judging it solely as a film, I would have to say this movie is visually stunning with its picturesque shots, forging a solid work of cinematography that reminds me of oil paintings.  The script is intriguing at times but it leaves a bad taste in my mouth, much like baby food would (don't ask why I would try baby food).  Very redundant and childish, it leaves nothing to the imagination and force feeds the audience it's plot.  One of the keys to a good film or story is its ability to keep the audience guessing, giving a sense of mystery and anticipation.  This script did not deliver and the movie did drag on at times.

Lots of nice performances.  Lots of nice art direction, but we've seen it all before.  It would have been fun if it were ninety minutes long.  As it was, it was an endless series of sword and sorcery been-there-seen-that and then and then and thens.  Boring and assaultive. Maybe for the religious Tolkein freaks....

ipc-title__text: Bad casting and no fluidity; overall, quite poor
ipc-html-content-inner-div: This movie had absolutely no flow to it whatsoever.  The character playing Sam was grossly overweight and looked more like he belonged in a candy store than among elite fighters in the Fellowship.  The cinematography was disappointing, and the special effects have been better elsewhere.  It was 3 hours worth of substandard, predictable fight scenes.  It certainly doesn't live up to the hype.

I had high expectations going in to see this movie.. I saw reviews... I thought I'd love it...  WRONGIt was SOoooo long and and I ate my nachos right at the beginning and so I didn't even have them to fall back on.  I even caught my brother playing on SNAKE on his mobile phone as an alternative to watching this movie.The acting was good, the scenery was nice.. the effects were great but I didn't get the wizard language and it just didn't grip me.I got so sick of the main guy whining and whinging about the ring.. they'd all cry and then have a group hug and then cry some more.
I usually like movies that are rated highly with the exception of this one. I can't believe they're making another 2 of these :(

Sorry all, but this movie is really bad.  There are some beautiful scenes, but a number that are ridiculous.  The acting was mediocre and I didn't care about the trek to throw the ring into the volcano.  It took way too long to get to that point.  Sorry, but Potter is a hundred times better as a film.

The film is beautifully photographed and well casted.  The depiction of the shire is wonderful.  BUT, there is broad use of the cheapest kind of emotional manipulation, which is not used in the book; and an abundance of violence, which is not as significant in the book.  Overall, I found the film a great disappointment. To my mind, it is not true to the sense of the Trilogy. If you loved the imaginary world of the Trilogy, you might think twice about seeing this film.  This film, in the second half, has more the flavor of an overwrought special-effects action picture.

i just sat there waiting for three hours, hoping that i would be somewhat concerned about what happened on the screen... never got that far. it all felt so plastic, so animated, so lacking of atmosphere. i sat there sometimes blushing in shame, sometimes found myself yelling out in disappointment, sometimes just making faces like in deep agony. but i'm glad so many found the movie great even though i didn't. i guess that's far more important in a utilitarian way of seeing things. personally i'm looking forward to second one, and will force myself to watch this disappointment once again to see if i'm just mistaken.

i can't believe this movie has been out only a few weeks and already it's at number one in the IMDb list? are people nuts? lord of the rings is better than citizen kane?what a load of dross. overlong, monotonous, a vacuous special-effects bonanza with no soul and no substance. ever imagine a video game where you pop the CD-ROM into your machine/console, and then it just plays for 3 long, long hours, and you can't do anything to influence or direct the action? this movie is like that. a "visual feast" it may be - too bad i felt bulimic after watching it.

ipc-title__text: Don't believe the hype.  This movie SUCKS
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Don't fall into the trap that all of these middle earth trolls, wizards and goblins set.  Lord of the Rings is not a good movie.(1) The direction is shoddy.  I don't think Peter Jackson has made a good movie yet.  The editing and pace or LOTR is TV mini-series caliber at best.(2) A lot of the acting is sub-par.  I think Elijah Wood is a fine actor and is OK with this goofy script, but the other 3 Hobbits are bad.  Sean Astin, is it Rudy or Sam?  As for the other two, I think I saw better acting in Monty Python's "Holy Grail".  Other than Ian McKellen, the rest of the actors wallow in the poorly written "Middle-Earth"/English/Irish/New England accented dialouge.(3) Some of the special effects were cheap.  I liked the battle scenes and the the CGI monsters, but every scene with a Hobbit that had to address a size issue was laughable.  The perspective trick never worked because the actor's line of sight was almost always off.  If this wasn't used, the characters didn't even appear to be in the same room at the same time. Best of all, was the use of midget doubles when the camera angles were far enough away.  IT WAS OBVIOUS!  I've scene better doubles in bad karate movies.So all of you guys who think this is "the greatest movie ever made" need to go back down in your parent's basement and finish your game of "Dungeons and Dragons".  If you've seen this movie more than once, you need a life.

ipc-title__text: In one word all I can say is WOW!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I went to see Lord of The Rings today and my heart is still beating from excitement. My mind is still on high candy eye ! Peter Jackson has done the impossible in my opinion made a film that is better than Star Wars (which I never liked anyway). The action sequences are enthrailling, the scenery is beautiful and the storyline is so memorizing and attention grabbing you won't move from your seat. Elijah Wood is great as Frodo, he's my pick for Best Actor this year. Viggo Mortsen as Stryder is a solider in this movie, he just goes G.I. style the whole movie. I can't wait for the second movie and to see it again. **** out of ****.

ipc-title__text: A peice of absolute epic garbage.
ipc-html-content-inner-div:
There are pretty much two ideas of this film, one it's great, two it's ok-- the books are better. However both are quite mistaken, quite mistaken indeed.This movie is trash, absolute and utter trash.Not that the books are better, which they are, or that this movie sways to far away from them, which it does as well, but that this film is, well, just plain bad.Now visually, it's somewhat good, some scenes are great, most are normal, in fact quite a few are terrible, but I'll just says it's ok.
The acting, well, the acting never really matters to me, so I won't bother to talk about it.The sound, is, probably the best part about it, which, however, isn't saying much.The story is decent, I was never much a fan of the story, even in the book, to begin with but I guess it will do.My problem lies in the pacing.The film is paced horrendously bad. The book had perfect pacing, but here they screwed it all up, they make the long sense short, the short scenes long, and the best scenes (for the most part) absent.Also the film goes on and on forever, like the ending of AI, the movie wants to end it's self but doesn't seem to be able to thanks to the fact of the director, the editor, the screenplay, studio, source material and everything else.In fact at the end of each and every scene I felt the movie wanted to end. Every five minutes a found a new perfect ending, but none of them were used, it went on and on and on.Another problem (once again due to pacing) is the fact that the film has no idea how to switch gears, smoothly. It has no clue how to go from fast and exciting, slow and poetic, intense and emotional, and just plain intense.
We feel like we're watching a made-for-TV movie, without the commercials.
I think that maybe it would be better for business- instead of putting in sly product placements just every five minutes place in a well meaning two minute commercial break. Then all of us could just enjoy the film and blame this last point on the commercials instead of the stupidity of those who made it, which is the only place I'm left to place the blame.
I understand that making three movies and once is a hard thing to do, in fact I understand that making one movie and once is a hard thing to do, but why is the question I'm asking, why? The only reasons I could come up with were- a) the studio couldn't afford three separate films, in which case none of them should've been made, period. Or- b)as a simply, good old fashioned, Cecil B. Demillian marketing ploy, a publicity stunt and if such is the case I will never just shrug it off and say, well it's because of the schedule, as everyone seems to state.Who knows maybe the second and third films will be greater. I do not anticipate returning but accept that I must, as my mother is a great fan of this one, and will drag me kicking and screaming to see it, at least I think she will.I got a bad feeling about this film when I heard that J R.R. Tolkien's grandson was disowned by good ole dad by supporting the making of this film, and to tell the truth I think it was a good move, in fact  I might've done it myself had I knew they it would've been like this!The book was a about fantasy, the movie about money, the book about a world, the movie about action, the book about life, the movie about death.
Now maybe some people like to see those things on a film, I am quite a big fan of huge multi-million dollar epics, and I love to view death/violence/carnage on screen- usually, but I hate action, in fact, it doesn't excite me in the least, it usually just gives me a headache, and that's at this films core, and thus all I got from this film was an immense craving for aspirin- not a good sign, if you ask me.

ipc-title__text: Tolkiens will love it, but for the rest of the planet there's always Star Wars
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I've seen this film twice.  The first time was on the preview night and I so hated the film that I wrote this 1000-word review venting why, but it was never posted (probably too offensive to hobbits, elves and dwarves). Anyway saw it again cause of friends wanting to see it, less enthusiastic to slam the movie now as I slept through the middle hour and awoke for the end and got into all the battles.  The film was really well cast Gandalf, Frodo, the elves and Strider were excellent. No character development however -- I couldn't tell Boromir and Strider apart the first time I saw the film, and the love scene between Strider and the Liv Tyler elf was ridiculously chaste, as if a cuddly hobbit imagined it while stealing vegetables (hobbits are so troublesome they step on peoples flowers and steal their broccoli). The orcs were wonderfully gruesome and the headless riders were pretty cool. From people I've talked to those that read the books and like role-playing games totally love the movie. If you hate the books you'll probably hate the movie -- Sam does seem to be in love with Frodo. I never read the books so I was just judging the movie on its own merits -- the effects were spectacular but I would have prefered less effects and more acting (especially with that cast!). I would have liked more humour as well (I think the movie has just one good laugh). The way the film ended also seemed too abrupt -- the second time I saw it I understood it better so it was O.K. but you shouldn't need to see a film like this twice to grasp the ending (Empire Strikes Back had a cliffhanger ending but it left you wanting more -- this just made me want to get out of my seat). In general, I thought it was way too faithful to the book (too literal) and lacked a more personal vision. I also hated the score, nostalgic and sentimental whenever Elijah Wood was busy looking earnest and overwhelmed; operatic and grandiose during the endless fight scenes, frenetic action sequences with cuts every couple of eye blinks. Probably won't see the sequels as I have the feeling I'll probably want to punch Frodo in the face by the end.

ipc-title__text: This is simply a bad movie
ipc-html-content-inner-div: As I write, Fellowship of the Rings is rated as the number one movie of all time on IMDb.  This can only be the result of early and eager voting by the cult that surrounds the book itself.  The movie itself is actually rather poor.Fans view this movie as the first installment of a grand epic.  Far from it! FOTR is without substance, formulaic... just a surreal montage of unexplained magic.Whatever devotees of the book may feel, those of us who have not read the book will find the story-line to be weak and uninspiring, and the characters to be not worthy of our empathy.The director places us so deeply inside the fight scenes that they are merely a whirlwind of activity, with no real perspective.  It is a chaos from which the protagonists emerge as the lucky survivors, chosen by God Hollywood.What makes it worst is the prevalence of magic.  I'm sure magic must be what it is all about for the fans of the books, but it must be handled better than this.  Here, the fantasy is so rich and takes us so far away from reality that we simply can't relate.  An unexplained magic leaves on the brink of an unstoppable apocalypse, an unexplained magic conjures up fabulous rescues for our heroes -- an unexplained magic can simply make any terrible or wonderful thing happen, without warning, at any moment.  What a horrible, random, unreal world in which to live!  People aren't even themselves, as an unexplained magic can possess and control them, as well.A real epic develops characters with humanity, that rise up against a great challenge in a context that we understand.  They can be relatively real like Braveheart or Gladiator, or they can be fantastic like the Star Wars series, but they must tell a coherent, inspiring and dramatic story.  FOTR does none of the above.Finally, when I spend three hours in a movie theatre watching a so-called epic, I would like the movie to have an actual climactic ending.  It matters not to me that this is the first of three books.  When this film ends it is clear that it is nothing more than an installment, not a story in-and-of-itself.  This does not make for a satisfying film-going experience.For fans of the books, the other reviews seem to indicate that they will likely pee with glee upon seeing the beloved Tolkein on the silver screen. For the rest of us, this movie is a real waste.

ipc-title__text: Follows the strengths and flaws of the book
ipc-html-content-inner-div: As a sad fan of fantasy fiction, but someone who thought the book of "The Lord of the Rings" was overrated, this film came pretty much up to expectations. It has much the same strengths (beautiful scenery and detail) as well as a couple of its own (great special effects, fight scenes, performances from Ian McKellen and Christopher Lee). It also has the same big flaw, the plot. It took me a couple of times to get past the first book as the plot meanders. Unfortunately the film is the same, and after a while, as someone  lese has pointed out, it just turns into a "Dungeons and Dragons" game with a number of scenarios which the heroes have to fight or puzzle their way out of. Still worth seeing as, like the book, the plot is only part of the point. The setting, scenery and special effects are superb and there are truly some moments of terror especially near the beginning. The second film, like the second book, will hopefully be better. It's certainly not the best film of all time.7 out of 10

I guess I am one of those people who prefer the book to the movie.  It was hard for me to find something to like about this flick.  The score was cliched, the sound mix muddy (overwhelming some spoken lines), and apart from the fantastic scenery, the cinematography was like that of a Gap commercial.I could run down the liberties taken from the plot and characters of the book, but since there were so many, I am trying to judge this as a 'stand-alone' enterprise.  Aspiring to Ben-Hur proportions, it just doesn't build any suspense or drama....I think mostly because of the multiple overblown 'moments' in the movie.It was mildly entertaining, but not anything groundbreaking.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring", the first movie in "The Lord of the Rings" trilogy, is a spectacular movie epic in every way. This film succeeds in all departments: acting, directing, writing, cinematography, editing, art direction, costume design, music score, sound, and special effects. You name it. The big name cast that takes part in this outstanding motion picture includes Elijah Wood, Sean Astin, Cate Blanchett, Liv Tyler, Ian McKellen, and Christopher Lee. They (along with others) play characters that were originated by J.R.R. Tolkien, the author of "The Lord of the Rings" books, and brought to life by director Peter Jackson (who shot this and the two "Lord of the Rings" sequels simultaneously in his native New Zealand). This, along with "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone", stand head and shoulders above all the other 2001 movies. But I don't want to say that "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is the best movie of 2001 yet. Right now it is (with "Harry Potter" at #2), but there are still a few other 2001 releases that I want to see that I haven't seen yet (like "Black Hawk Down" and "Gosford Park"), so probably a month or two from now I will know for sure if this terrific fantasy/adventure will finish on top as my favorite movie of 2001. But what a fantastic movie this was.
**** (out of four)

What I appreciate most about "Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is how, from the very beginning, it sits you down and just starts shamelessly pummeling you with the story of the rings and Middle Earth. There's this cool confidence evident in all of it, like the film is alive and believes in itself. The opening montage, the prologue that explains the history of the ring, is as good an excuse to not walk into a movie late as there has ever been. What follows is, in terms of modern filmmaking, a revolution. Peter Jackson leaves nothing to chance. He doesn't believe in the saying, 'you can't please everyone.' His first installment of the trilogy makes sure a good time is had by all. It's the ultimate in film entertainment.
"Ring" has the inside track to not only get nominated for the Best Picture Oscar, but to win. Like "Gladiator" last year, "Ring" is the greatest overall achievement in filmmaking of the year. Its only legitimate acting nominee would be Ian McKellen, who deserves a Supporting Role nomination. If not, there is a precedent for films winning BP without any acting nominations. "The Last Emperor" did it in '87. Before that you have to go waaay back to the 50s for "Greatest Show on Earth," "Around the World in 80 Days," and "Gigi" to find others who accomplished this feat. It hasn't happened much, but it could happen again this year.Grade for "Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring": A

Watching Lord of the Rings is at once a mesmerizing and fascinating experience. Even if you've never read any of the books, the story is woven in such a delicious, viewer-friendly manner that even the most curmudgeonly of us will appreciate the tale.The Lord of the Rings trilogy (actually four books, if you include the prequel The Hobbit) tells the tale of the quest to return an all-powerful (and all-evil) ring to the fire from whence it was forged in an effort to destroy it forever. J. R. R. Tolkien's books are very rich with detail, particularly with historical detail. The world of Middle earth is populated by all sorts of creatures, and man is not yet the dominating species. In Tolkien's world, sorcery, might, and pastoral settings all exist  together, albeit not always in perfect harmony. The first several minutes of the 178-minute movie (subtitled The Fellowship of the Ring, the title of the first book in the series) describes the terrible history of the One Ring. If someone had not read the books, it might be difficult for them to comprehend the story; thankfully, the startling special effects and brisk storytelling make it all worthwhile and informative.In short, here's how the tale unfolds. Back in the old days, the ultimate evil being Sauron forged a series of powerful rings. Some he gave to the Elvish race (known for their wisdom). Some he gave to Men. Some he gave to Dwarves (known for their strength and courage). But there was one Ring that was designed to bind all of the others together, to be as strong as all the others combined. With this ring, one could rule all of Middle Earth. But the evil Sauron was defeated by Men, and his hand (well, the hand of his physical being) was chopped off; a Man recovered the Ring, but fell prey to its power. The Ring eventually sunk to the bottom of a river, where it was recovered by an eerie creature named Gollum, who also fell prey to its allure. And from this creature, the tiny Hobbit Bilbo Baggins acquired the Ring, not knowing its power and keeping it to himself for 60 years. Bilbo gives the Ring to his nephew, Frodo Baggins.When the Ring's existence is confirmed, a meeting involving all of the creatures of Middle Earth is convened in the Elvish home of Elron, the lord of the Elves. It is decided that the Ring must be returned to the peak of Mount Doom, where it must then be cast into the fires that made it (and where it can be unmade). Frodo volunteers for the horrible task, and representatives from each of the major species in Middle Earth are assembled to aid him in his quest: Aragorn and Boromir from the land of Men; Leglolas the Elf; Gimli the Dwarf; Gandalf the wizard; and the Hobbits, Frodo, Samwise, Peregrin, and Merry. These nine are chosen to travel the great distance to the land of evil, and cast the ring back.Quite a daunting task, isn't it? And while all of this is going on, the evil of Sauron is aware that the Ring exists, and he is preparing his armies for his own quest - recover the Ring at all costs. Luckily, the good guys have some all-stars on their side. Gandalf (played very memorably by Ian McKellen) is more than just a circus magician - he's one of the most powerful wizards in history (that's not common knowledge at the outset, at least not to the naive Hobbits, but it's apparent rather quickly). Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen) is more than a mere Ranger, he's also of noble blood, and has the courage of a thousand lions. These two leaders are the soul and minds of the Fellowship. But the story's focus is on the tiny Ringbearer, Frodo. You see, carrying this ring isn't quite the same as, for example, carrying a wedding ring up the aisle to the about-to-be-wed. Frodo is drawn to the ring but still has such amazing inner strength that he can stick to his mission. He knows its power, and as he gets closer and closer to Mount Doom the pressure of carrying the jewelry is absolutely overwhelming. It's as if you or I walked around the office carrying a Volkswagen.Besides the story, there are two other intangible stars at work here: the special effects and the makeup/costumery. There's one particular scene in which Gandalf rides a giant bird (an eagle, perhaps) to safety. My mind immediately assumed this could happen; but upon reflection I believe that this was wizardry of another time, another example of the magnificence of special effects. Some of the scenes are absolutely jaw-dropping. The Fellowship must travel through the Mines of Moria; they tackle the precipice of a giant snow-covered mountain; they hike over marshes and through forests. And at no point does one think that all of this is make-believe.Another asset is the cinematography. Gandalf is a human, although a tall one in the books. The Hobbits are halflings, or little people - they're much smaller than humans. Their homes are smaller, and Gandalf has to duck to enter. But side by side, Gandalf and Bilbo look exactly as they should - Gandalf perhaps six feet tall, and Bilbo perhaps four. Not bad when you consider both roles are played by grown men (Bilbo is played by Ian Bannen)!
And the acting! Mortensen as Aragon! John Rhys-Davies as Gimli the Dwarf! The great Christopher Lee as Saruman the White, a fellow wizard of Gandalf! Sean Bean as Boromir!  And the actresses are even better. Liv Tyler as Arwen the elf and Cate Blanchett as the Lady Galadriel are absolutely stunning. These are not just beautiful women playing ethereal roles; their screen presence is off the charts. The only downside to the acting is Elijah Wood as Frodo. Throughout the movie, he looked like a deer caught in headlights, constantly stunned and shocked. Wood's never been a particularly good actor, and his limitations are unfortunately readily amplified by this major role. But he's not horribly miscast, either. Most of the time, the action in the movie is so intense you forget what a dull performance he's turning in.
I've read all of the books, so of course I knew what to expect here. The friend I went to the movie with had not read the books, so I asked her if she found it boring, uninteresting, or confusing. She answered in the negative, surprising considering the length of the film. But here's something you can expect, if you've not read these wonderful books. There are three books, of course, and the other two movies have been filmed already. The ending of this film does not tie everything up neatly (as the first book did not). The filmmakers faced a very difficult task in ending the movie, and they chose to stick with the book's ending (which I certainly will not reveal here). But please, if you watch this film, realize there are two more to come, and that the ending of this is also the beginning to the next one. There are plenty of intense scenes in the movie, probably too intense for very young kids. This is NOT a children's story (the books certainly weren't, either), although it's one that can be enjoyed by all. If I had kids, I would be reading these books to them as often as possible. This is epic storytelling at its absolute best. There is never a slow moment in the movie (or the books). The movie is a masterpiece, one of the finest examples of moviemaking we've seen in a long, long time.

I swear every line of dialogue in this film was spoken with the gravity appropriate to the Constitution or the Old Testament.  Every scene had the portent of Christ's ascension into heaven.  There was very little down time or joy, except in the beginning during the birthday celebration.To those who say the film was stylish, I say it certainly had a lot of black in it.CGI was good, my favorite shots being the fireworks that turn into a swooping dragon and the flooding river in the shape of galloping horses.Basically, I got tuckered out by every scene starting with Gandalf saying "This is the mighty forest such-and-such" and then a minute later "Oh, no, that beast is the mighty such-and-such, who lives on the blood of others." The plot felt like a greatest hits sampling of the book.  I cared very little for any of the characters.Elijah Wood kept me fascinated.  He has a great face.

I was a moderate admirer of Tolkein.  I read the Hobbit and the first and third books of the trilogy.  I never really got in to the world of Middle Earth to the same level as the scores of D&D folks, but I consider myself a fan.  That said, this movie left me feeling flat and uninspired.  The books were not written to tell a story, they just existed, just as history books don't necessarily have a moral or plot.  The movie however is trying to concoct a moral in this tale.  The fellowship is far to thin to carry me along.  I didn't care for any of the characters and the dialouge seemed very rigid and uninspired.  Overall it wasn't a bad movie, and I suspect if the editing was a little tighter and about 30 minutes was trimmed off the end, I would call it a success.  As of now, I can only recommend for the super fans, and suspect that if the second one isn't improved it will bomb.

Firstly i wanna say that i though The Fellowship of the Rigns (TFOTR) was a good movie. In fact ill go as far to say a "great" movie but the greatest or anything over 7 out of ten NO WAY My first problem with this film is its pacing and structure. The film climaxes in the wrong spot ! and then preceeds this with boring unpolished work that just detracts from the overall film. This is also the reason for its incomprehensible length. 3 hours !! why ? It just gets lost in a lot of stuff that could have been cut and maybee saved for the dvd, but to put it all in a final release like this is stupid. By this i am refering to the final battle on the hill, the scene with kate blanchet etc. My second major gripe is the overuse of Special effects. Ok the first 10 minutes blew me away totally especially those shots of the battle WOW amazing. also the scene with the big ogre thing in the caves. That was extreemly well done. Apart from this effects are used way too often and in doing this the good bits loose their impact. The best form of film suspense and creativity is subtlety and utilising the screen to stir the imagination. In this film we see a gross hollywood action style overuse of effects. Whether this is to keep it true to the book i dont know but it just ruins the effect of the good special effects and computer graphics sequences. having said all this i think someone will do what they did with starwars episode one and re-cut the film. Also: Georgie Lucas and ILM better get their arses in gear cause some of the special effects in this film blow star wars episode one off the map. But that is to be expected considering the time gap between both. I hope we get blown off the planet again with episode 2 and then taken even further with the two towers the sequal to this film

Well not exactly but the movie does not deserve a top score. I cannot help but to compare the LOTR and The Wheel of Time. LOTR is sterile when compared to the world and colour of the Wheel of Time. ipc-title__text: I thought it would never end
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Overall, I felt Lord of the Rings was a decent movie; however, it was ruined by the fact that it went on-and-on-and-on for nearly three hours.   At the two hour point, having already slipped out to use the restroom once, I found myself squirming in my chair hoping somebody would kill him just so we could end the misery!The imagery is very good, and for the most part, so is the acting.  There is a great deal of camera movement, especially during the "fight scenes", so if your susceptible to nausea from this (such as in Blair Witch), at least try sitting towards the back.I realize cutting this film down to two hours may be considered by some to be like cutting the Book of Revelations from the Bible, but...the movie is way too long, the climax happens a dozen too many times, and I found myself losing interest in the whole thing.Rating:  4 out of 10

Technologically stunning and often well-acted, the movie was about an hour too long. I make no comment about the novel from which the story was taken, as I have not read it. But the film rarely succeeds in capturing any real attachment to its characters or concern for their fate. Frodo, the hobbit who is the central character, spends altogether too much time staring into space. The backgrounds, which appear to be generated by computer, are often very beautiful and reveal a vivid visual imagination. The battle scenes are likewise very imaginatively "staged." But they are so numerous and so overwhelming, both visually and sonically, that they soon become much of a muchness. I hope that the producers have the good sense to leave more of the sequels on the cutting-room floor.

ipc-title__text: now THAT'S what I call a movie !!!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I'm 40, have read LOTR 5 times since age 12, most recently a few weeks ago. I've waited 28 years for this film and was prepared to be disappointed. Instead, every sight, scene and sound that I imagined in my mind's eye was far surpassed by this film.  Some characters are missing, some dialogue is dropped - sometimes for no good reason.  A scene or two is changed from the book just for the sake of more action.  Saruman's motivation is changed, they don't get their elven cloaks, no Barrowwights, etc.Guess what ?  It doesn't matter.  In fact, when you realize that 3 hours has flown by and the movie is over you don't worry about what's not in, you worry about how you are gonna wait a year for the next one.  No, I take that back.  I'm worried about when I can see it again.  There was no way to keep everything in without going well over 3 hours - just be glad the studio let them do the full 3.This is Braveheart, The 12th Warrior, Last of the Mohicans, Excalibur and a couple of monster movies all rolled into one.  And PLEASE, see this in the best theater you can find, one with a big screen AND great sound.  It needs and deserves the best environment you can find.  God, just something simple like the sound of the horses was scary.A very rare 10 from this viewer.

I am one of those people who never read. I simply cannot pick up a book and last 10 pages without falling asleep. I am a movie buff, plain and simple. After hearing the hype about J.R.R. Tolkien's classic story, I had to watch and see for myself.I have always been a big fan of fantasy movies, the larger the cast of characters, the better. The Fellowship of the Ring certainly has that - and much more. I am now fascinated dwellers of Middle Earth - the Dwarves, Elves, Hobbits, Orcs, Wizards, Warriors - everyone of them.Peter Jackson has done a wonderful job in transforming words to movement, suffice to say that this movie makes me want to pick up the book and read (hopefully I'll reach page 20). I thoroughly enjoyed the fight scenes, the intricate dialogue, the comradarie, the betrayals and not forgetting, the effects. Never a dull moment, this movie has definitely lived up to my expectations.Sure, the Fellowship of the Ring will have its fair share of detractors, but I dare say that nothing will stop this movie franchise from becoming the largest ever or at least get on par with the original Star Wars Trilogy. Just one wish - An Oscar Nomination for Sir Ian McKellen please?

ipc-title__text: The best fantasy film since the original Star Wars!
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I went into this film expecting to like it, the buzz was good and the story is weel known. Little did I think that I would be blown away so much that I have not left a theater as excited about a movie since I was a kid after I saw Star Wars. Most people are focusing on the special effects, which are remarkable, but I think that the film succeeds on all levels,most fantasy films these days are fx extravanganzas and are entertaining, but are not remembered soon after, they are just fun video games. Peter Jackson must have really loved this story, alot of care went into the producing of this story. Yes it is an adventure,full of action and thrills, but it takes itself seriously,Jackson has created a whole world, not just a bunch of action set pieces. Star Wars in 1977 felt that way, earnest and completely emerses the viewer into its world, no movie since has had done that as successfully until now, Bravo to Mr. Jackson and everyone involved in the making of Fellowship. Finally a movie that will make a huge amount of money, but will actually deserve it! Run, don't walk to see it!

The one thing this movie does not do is transcend the sword and sorcery genre.  The first 2 hours or so were like a play put on at a Ren Faire, only with a really high budget.  It got better from there.  By the end of the movie, I no longer was rooting for the Ring Wraths to just get the damn ring so we could go home.  Part of that animosity comes from the fact that I had a bad headache for a long part of the movie.  At least three people I know of got headaches from the way the movie was filmed.  Take some advil before you go.This isn't a horrible movie.  There are good things in it.  However, it isn't any sort of all time classic unless you're a huge fan of the genre. You'll either see this ten times and go on and on about how great it was or leave wondering what all of the fuss was about.

ipc-title__text: Why Waste Time on a Story When You Can Have Fights?
ipc-html-content-inner-div: I just saw this two days ago.  I have never read the books and so I was an empty slate ready to fall into the fantasy world of The Ring.  I enjoyed the film and was fairly easily entertained for the three hours.  They did an outstanding job of creating the terrain, peoples, and buildings of an unearthly place.  I really felt like I was watching the goings-on of another world.  In my opinion, the acting, casting, and music were all good.Yet, the movie left me with somewhat of any empty and unconvinced feeling. The character development was really lacking.  Although I watched them for 3 hours, I left feeling like I didn't get to know the characters.  I REALLY wanted to like Frodo and root for him, but I don't think they did a great job of endearing him to the audience.  Without that, you start caring less about his plight.  I also felt that they needed to develop the friendships in the film.  When you see a portrayal of a great friendship, it reminds you of your own good friends and what they've meant and done for you.  This draws you more into the story.  The greatest failure here is with Frodo and Sam.  To an uninitiated viewer like me, Sam comes across as an annoying tag-along, when I think he's supposed to be a staunch friend.I agree with the previous reviewer who wrote that deep-down this was an epic action film, not an epic fantasy film.  After awhile I began to feel that I was watching a group of wooden characters, assembled together as the glue used to transition from action sequence to action sequence.  While the action sequences were fabulous, they lacked real meaning due to the weak characters.  I even detected in some of the monster sequences a bit of that campy, slasher movie feel.  A little too Freddy Krueger or Michael Jackson Thriller-ish.The movie spends too much time trying to entertain with monsters and fights and not enough with characters.  This is the movie's real failure to achieve greatness.  The director's motto seemed to be "Why waste time on a good story when you can have action and fights?"  They took an uncommon story and made an all-too-common film out of it.

I will not join the parade of favorable reviews of this film.Lord of the Rings was at least an hour too long.  More attention should have been paid to tight, cogent screen writing.  Moreover, unless one familiar with the books, the movie is hard to follow as the development of many of the characters in the latter part of the movie was  sorrowfully lacking. Perhaps the film was attempting to take on too large of a project, resulting in a "classic" film for those who read the books.The acting was rich and beautiful, especially considering the limitations place on the actors by the script.  For the most part, the special effects were first rate.  However, there were inconsistencies in the computer generated character size disparities.  While for the most part the computer worked fine, at others it failed miserably.  Far too often, for example, Frodo and Gandalf appear almost the same size.What kept this from becoming a great film was its inability to appeal to all moviegoers with a screenplay that stands on its own without relying on the viewers' knowledge of J.R.R. Tolkien's works.

Best visual effects, best environment just like i imagined in my brain... I've read this book six times... Not-bad, not-good musics.. But what about the scenario? No, it is awful.. Jackson cut lots of key scenes from film. E.g, Gandalf is not a Power-Ranger and Saruman is not a Power-Ranger bad guy. This film does NOT give the feeling of Fellowship and brotherhood of the ring like in the book. I can exactly name this film as Peter Jackson's Lord of The Rings....

I cannot believe that this is the #1 rated movie on this site!  I have seen at least three movies this year that I thought were waaay better!  Was ANYONE else at all bored during this film?This'll get me killed:  I picked up my ticket stub at one point and thought about sneaking into Harry Potter, I was so bored.

ipc-title__text: If I wanted to see 3-hour long theatrical trailer, I'd rent Star Wars

Make this movie at least a little boring, with some substance, a little more attention to detail and, please, bring those "people" down to earth so I can relate to them!!! So I don't have to sit in the movie theater and wish that I could be watching this on DVD and be taking a lot of breaks. I feel like I am in an episode of the twilight zone, where everyone is oblivious to the obvious except for me.  No matter what I say, I can't convince anyone of the truth, the horrible horrible truth....  Dear god, what happened to you all?Last night I spent three hours sitting in a theatre which, by the way, was mostly empty, watching the most overhyped movie since The Phantom Menace. Lord of The Rings was mediocre at best.  It served it's genre well with lots of swords and sorcery, but as far as it's overall quality, it was SEVERELY lacking.  The story runs like an '87 Honda Prelude.  It takes an hour to get up to 55mph.  The first hour and a half is spent setting up what turns out to be a NON-ENDING.  We are forced to follow young Frodo and his pack of badly developed and badly directed companions along a seemingly endless journey to... Well, I'll let YOU see for yourself.  The trip is punctuated by short bursts of action that seem to do little more than whet your appetite for SOMETHING - ANYTHING to happen.  I got to see SHREK shot in the head with an arrow in one underground battle. Who was in charge of THAT CGI sequence?The tools and materials for a top notch film are all here.  Great actors, fantastic sets and beautifully desinged costumes along with a solid story. Something went terribly wrong in the storyboarding stage, however.  The film has no structure.  There is no first, second and third act.  Instead there are a couple of short fight scenes and an unresolved ending.  None of the combat sequences is any more or less grand in scale, so the film never reaches any kind of climax.  I found myself waitng, waiting and waiting some more for a signal that the film was at it's halfway point, a signal that never came.  There was a collective groan of both disgust and ticked-offedness when the ending FINALLY rolled around.  I would equate the feeling to waiting in line at Universal Studios for three hours to go on a thrill ride that EVERYONE has been RAVING about.  You get on the ride and wind up watching anamatrons sing "It's a small world after all."  You want your money back.  A properly executed trilogy is exemplified in STAR WARS. Here you have three separate films revolving around a central story.  Each film has a climax and a resolution and can stand on it's own.  It seems that for any kind of satisfaction with the LOTR trilogy, we are going to have top sit through all nine hours of the completed set.  I don't know what is wrong with everyone, you all must be mad because this film is NOT worth a 9.6 rating.  It's worth a 7 at BEST.  It seems that all of you Tolkein fans out there just blindly accept whatever comes your way.  The industry really gave you all a hype enema and I guess the general feeling out there in 'fantasy world' was "Thank you sir! May I have another?"  Wake up, pull your heads out of the 'dungeon' and move out of the basement.  The reality is, Hollywood stole your money on this one.  I have to go now, it's time to check up on Jar Jar Binks to see how he is going to ruin ANOTHER STAR WARS film.  Keep it real.

ipc-title__text: Great Fantasy, but only a Fantasy of Greatness
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Don't get me wrong.  I liked this film a lot, but was disappointed at what was slashed from the books, as well as what was changed.  First of all: they shouldn't have cut the barrow-wight.  It would have been a great opportunity to show yet another monster of Middle-Earth.  And they could have found a way out besides through Tom Bombadil, who was rightfully cut out.  They should not have cut out the incident concerning blindfolding in Lorien. It's critical to the understanding of the relationships between the races. But the biggest problem I had between book and film was where they introduced Gollum's pursuit of the Fellowship.  In the books, Gollum picks up their trail beginning in Lorien, after coming out of Moria.  Having him begin within Moria introduces far too many plot holes: how did he get INTO the mines?  If they knew exactly where Gollum was, why didn't they apprehend or kill him?  How did Gollum avoid the Orcs, Trolls, and other dangers? And how does he eventually leave Moria?  Start his pursuit in Lorien, and problems are solved. Enough with the negative stuff.  What is in the movie is VERY good.  The locations and visuals are mind-blowing, and the performances by the actors is astounding.  For some reason, the most striking performance to me was Christopher Lee as Saruman, followed shortly by Ian McKellen as Gandalf. Peter Jackson does a very good job at capturing a portion of the epic scope and grandeur of Tolkien's trilogy, and can foreseeably net himself an Oscar for the effort.  However, while this film could easily be the film of year for 2001 (I haven't seen much better this year), it is probably not one of, and certainly not THE greatest of all time, as today's glimpse at the Top 250 suggests.
No life, no cleverness, just never-ending fight against overwhelming forces of inept evil. Preposterous pontifications delivered by cartoonish characters are middle school deep.5/10 for visuals

ipc-title__text: 3-hour epic turns out to be a dud
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Boring is the `key' word to use in this film.  God, was it ever boring, especially near the end.   The thing I wished the director did was to edit lots of the unnecessary emotional parts of the film (i.e. death of Boromir) so it could have been shorten to 2.25-2.5 hours.  So, at least my short attention span would have been kept intact.  I have not read the book, so I cannot comment on the book to movie transfer. However I do agree with the comments made by Tolkien's son about the movie, when he said, `his father if alive would NOT have been impressed'.   A little advice, if you like me, and have no liking for fantasy type movies (by that I mean, movies that have elves, dwarfs, humans) avoid this movie at ALL costs.  I gave this movie a 2 (an extra 1 just cause the special effects were kinda cool!)

ipc-html-content-inner-div: I thought it was visually stunning, and Jackson did well. The first book is the weakest anyway, but I have never been so bored at the cinema! The movie was okay, the story never really pulled me in. Just not my thing. The special effects were top notch, state of the art - some of the best stuff in years that I've seen. But the whole movie was sort of not going anywhere with not a whole lot of plot to speak of, especially to a non-fantasy, non-Tolkien fan.

Like many, I have also read the books and was aware of the story and characters going into the film.  While the visuals, especially that stunning battle scene at the start of the film, were done to near perfection - it did miss the mark in a more fundamental way.Too much screen time was spent drawing out and languishing over several dramatic events of the film.  I found myself thinking, `Okay we know this guy is going to die, let's move the story along'.  For example, we see a character get hit with an arrow, muster strength to fight some more, then almost die, then get hit with another arrow, again muster more strength and fight again, then almost die, then get hit with yet another arrow, and tries to muster his strength again.  And to top it off this long drawn out scene is full of added elements that were not in the book.  The film was littered with examples like this (the character that almost drowns at the end of the film - also painfully drawn out.  Any time Frodo puts on the ring - painfully drawn out)Yes film is a medium different that that of a novel, but if Jackson wanted to make a three hour movie, he should have spend more screen time developing character and plot motivations.  This would keep the audience from getting lost and from asking, `why are our characters going to this place?', and `who is this guy?'.  Once characters and key plot point is properly setup with their motivations explained, then the drama will naturally come out, and it won't need the added drama effects, heavy sound and score to force the audience to feel a certain way.Jackson simply lets the characters and story get buried with the overuse of dramatic effects.  Very little time was spent developing Frodo and Sam, as likeable real characters.  They just appeared as cardboard cutouts borrowed from the Phantom Menace, with no real motivation and human connection to anyone else in the film.It's a good film to see once, but just for the special effects.

A Timeless Epic: A Review of The Lord of the Rings
The Lord of the Rings isn't just a movie, it's an experience. From the moment the familiar score washes over you, you're transported to Middle-earth, a world brimming with wonder, peril, and fellowship. Peter Jackson's vision for Tolkien's masterpiece is nothing short of phenomenal.The story follows a hobbit named Frodo Baggins who inherits the One Ring, an artifact of immense power coveted by the Dark Lord Sauron. Thrust into a perilous journey, Frodo joins a fellowship of hobbits, men, elves, dwarves, and a wizard to destroy the Ring in the fires of Mount Doom.The characters are the heart of this film. Frodo's innocence and determination are endearing, while Gandalf's wisdom and Aragorn's nobility inspire. The camaraderie between the fellowship is heartwarming, making their sacrifices all the more impactful.Visually, The Lord of the Rings is breathtaking. The sweeping landscapes, from the Shire's rolling hills to the fiery depths of Mordor, are a sight to behold. The creatures, from the majestic Balrog to the grotesque orcs, are brought to life with stunning special effects that hold up even today.The film's pacing is masterful. Despite its epic length, it never drags. There are moments of quiet contemplation balanced perfectly with thrilling action sequences. The battles are heart-stopping, showcasing the immense stakes of the war against Sauron.The Lord of the Rings is more than just a fantasy adventure. It's a story about friendship, courage, good versus evil, and the power of hope. It's a film that will stay with you long after the credits roll, leaving you yearning to return to Middle-earth.This is truly my all-time favorite film. It's a masterpiece that deserves every accolade it's received. A must-watch for any fantasy fan or anyone who appreciates a grand, epic adventure.

ipc-title__text: One of the best films of all time. No questions.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: When I was 10 years old, I watched the Lord of the Rings for the first time with my dad. 12 years later at the films re release, I still think that this is one of the best films ever. I went with my friend who has never seen the film before, and we both came out amazed and in awe. I've seen it before, but seeing it on the silver screen just brought so much more to life. Peter Jackson's cinematography brings this whole film to life, with the phenomenal book to screen translation. Me and my friend have already bought tickets to see the next 2, and I will write reviews for them as I see them. If you haven't seen it, watch it. That's all.

The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (Extended Edition)Fathom events put on a 3 day event over the weekend of June 8-10, 2024 to watch all 3 extended versions of the original trilogy in theaters. This review will have the slant of it being 23 years since the movie first hit theaters, and I've seen it dozens of times. I will say that I don't recall if I ever saw the extended editions in theaters; only on dvd, bluray or streaming.First, I have to say that it was amazing to be in a full movie theater again. After nearly a year of seeing tons of movies, this is only the second time that's happened to me, and the other one was a nerdy movie too. Go nerds!J R R Tolkien wrote the book throughout the 1940s, after the success of the Hobbit, calling on his own war time experiences during the Great War, and then WWII, which are noticed in the battle scenes, and the rise in nationalism.The first movie concentrates on the set up and exposition explaining the conflict, the characters, and the ring itself. Then it moves on to the quest to destroy the object that is bringing the world to war. In order to separate good from evil, races are created that look like monsters, so as not to draw comparisons to our own earthly chaos.One theme of the first film is that you can't use evil to defeat evil. It didn't work three thousand years ago, and it wasn't working in the present. The aforementioned fellowship falls apart because of this internal conflict. If a nuclear bomb is invented, but removed from the battlefield, don't run off with it to use it against your enemy, but destroy it. I definitely see pacifism in Tolkien's first book.Another theme I encountered is conservationism. The strongest, most courageous hobbits live in harmony with the land. The dwarves kept digging for treasure until something was unleashed that killed them all. That's pretty spot on for a metaphor, I would think.The world becomes so chaotic that even the "good and pure" elves are leaving. It's like they've given up. But having lived for thousands of years and seeing no improvements, I would probably leave too. ipc-title__text: Peter Jackson begins with a masterpiece in his iconic trilogy, The Fellowship of the Ring is a landmark in filmmaking
This is the movie that started it for me...
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Where do we even begin with a film like this that's been out for this long? Overall the plot is pretty simple. If you've ever read a book in the fantasy genre you can almost guess the arcs and concepts that will be presented in the film. A great evil threatens middle earth and a young hobbit, Frodo, completely unfit for the duty of saving the world is tasked with....well saving he world. What he lack in magical ability, strength, speed, power and just about anything else you'd need to actually save the world, he makes up in his willingness to sacrifice. Everybody else on the team brings their skills to the table to make up for what Mr. Frodo lacks.The fellowship is exactly the point of the project. A fellowship, between races and beliefs and peoples. The beauty of this film is in it's scope and simplicity. You want to be on that journey with them. Fighting for something worth fighting for. Knowing where the line between good and evil are and where exactly you stand in regard to that line.The action is adequate. Now I grew up on Donnie Yen, Michelle Yeoh and Jet Li. I was watching anime when I was 10 years old and had a rather developed sense of action sequences, yet the simpler performances put on in this film felt right. They fit with the narrative. The magic is muted and magical combat is severely limited. I could have used a bit more in this area but it was acceptable for the story being told. There were stakes, lives were lost and by the end of the film there are at least 2 scenes that happen that could make even the most manly man tear up a bit. Manly tears only of course. Just one rolling down the cheek. Unaccompanied. Solitary. Like the man crying it.In conclusion this is one of of my favorite films. It's a big inspiration to me and a major reason that I work in fantasy today. I cannot recommend this film more highly if they paid me.

The Lord of the Rings trilogy have to be the best three films ever made. They are masterpieces made when films used practical effects and a bit of CGI, and this truly makes these films works of art. From the set design, costumes, soundtrack, cast, special effects etc. Everything about these films is sheer perfection unrivalled. This is film making at its finest. I remember watching The Fellowship for the first time when I was about 11/12. I was utterly mesmerised. I'm now 32 and I have lost count of how many times I've rewatched these films. I will never get bored of them, they are timeless. The message of hope and bravery that runs throughout these films is beautiful and there are moments that move you to tears because that is just how utterly amazing and uplifting these films are. I'm currently about to begin the Two Towers and I cannot wait to be immersed in the world of Middle Earth once more! Thank you to everyone that made these films, and thank you J R R Tolkien for creating such an astoundingly beautiful universe for us all to enjoy in the first place.

ipc-title__text: "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring": A Magnificent Beginning to a Legendary Journey
ipc-html-content-inner-div: Peter Jackson's "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is a cinematic masterpiece that brings J. R. R. Tolkien's beloved fantasy epic to life with breathtaking scope, rich detail, and profound emotional resonance. Serving as the first installment in the monumental film trilogy, this adaptation captivates audiences with its dazzling visuals, compelling characters, and epic storytelling.The film follows the young hobbit Frodo Baggins, portrayed with earnestness and vulnerability by Elijah Wood, as he embarks on a perilous quest to destroy the One Ring, an artifact of immense power that threatens to plunge Middle-earth into darkness. Joined by a diverse fellowship of allies, including the wise wizard Gandalf (Ian McKellen), the noble warrior Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), and the loyal friends Samwise Gamgee (Sean Astin), Merry (Dominic Monaghan), and Pippin (Billy Boyd), Frodo sets out on a journey fraught with danger, adventure, and self-discovery.What sets "The Fellowship of the Ring" apart is its meticulous attention to detail and its unwavering commitment to capturing the spirit of Tolkien's literary masterpiece. From the idyllic landscapes of the Shire to the foreboding depths of the Mines of Moria, every corner of Middle-earth is brought to life with stunning visual effects, intricate set design, and evocative cinematography. The film's sweeping score, composed by Howard Shore, further enhances the immersive experience, transporting viewers to a world of magic and wonder.But beyond its technical achievements, "The Fellowship of the Ring" is also a deeply resonant and thematically rich film that explores timeless themes of friendship, courage, and the battle between good and evil. As Frodo and his companions face increasingly daunting challenges and moral dilemmas, the film delves into the complexities of heroism and sacrifice, reminding audiences of the power of hope and resilience in the face of adversity.Central to the film's success are the performances of its ensemble cast, who bring depth, humanity, and gravitas to their iconic roles. From Ian McKellen's commanding portrayal of Gandalf to Sean Bean's noble interpretation of Boromir, each actor imbues their character with a sense of authenticity and emotional depth that resonates long after the credits roll.In conclusion, "The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring" is a cinematic triumph-a film that transports viewers to a world of epic adventure, unforgettable characters, and timeless themes. Whether you're a fan of Tolkien's original novels or simply appreciate masterful storytelling and filmmaking, this is a movie that deserves its place among the greatest of all time-a true classic that will continue to inspire and enchant audiences for generations to come.

ipc-title__text: Timeless trilogy that will probably never be toped.
ipc-html-content-inner-div: First of all, it is difficult to write a separate review per single movie when in my mind it is one continuous story that only happens to be split up into three instances. Second, how can I even start to summarize my mixture of thoughts for a trilogy I have deeply loved ever since it came out over 20 years ago. Here is my attempt at it.I don't think recapping the plot is necessary as you can read the premise and I wouldn't dare spoil any more to people who are just about to watch the movies. The movie came out at a similar time as the Harry Potter movies did, to this day I can't really decide which franchise is a better adaptation of it's fantasy template (the books). At any case, I haven't seen a better adaptation ever since. The attention to detail when it comes to the sets, props, costumes is unmatched. If you ever watch the Making of features, you'll see that working on the Lord of the Rings was never just a 'job'. It was passion where everyone gave their 120% and it shows. Real sets which breath lore, real costumes that look weathered and worn, real acting from the cast.What makes the movies so compelling? At first we are shown the peacefulness of the Shire, as in the place worth fighting for. Then the heroes go on an epic journey trough realms of elves, dwarves, and various hostile creatures to defeat an evil that threatens to destroy the peacefulness of the inhabitants of this fantasy world. It is a formula that make such a compelling story, that it has been copied over and over since the original books came out. This was the original fantasy story. Each location you encounter feels like you are seeing just the tip of an iceberg of history and lore. Rightfully so, because Tolkien did indeed come up with a complete history for his fantasy world and then just placed his characters into it. Tolkiens dedication towards his fictional world is yet to be matched. Some might argue that modern Authors like Jordan or Sanderson compare or even top Tolkien. I don't agree but that is personal preference and a different kind of rant.Of course there have been changes made against the book to make the movies more cinematic. There are some nitpicky scenes and plot holes you might notice if you have seen the movie 20 times like me. I don't mind the differences though, because it gives me a reason to enjoy the books as much as the movies. I wouldn't dare call either better or worse, just different. To mention some differences, there were characters omitted, some characterization is a bit different. I Prefer book Frodo and Faramir, but Movie Aragorn and Sam. Book Frodo and Faramir are both more competent and wise than shown in the movie, Sam on the other hand seems to me as loyal simpleton in the books. Aragorn of the books is the sort of legendary hero whose character is already developed when we meet him. A king on the way to claim his throne. The Aragorn in the movies still needs to make this character development, and become the king which is IMO more compelling to watch.I don't think that there is anything I could write or say to persuade you to like these movies as much as I do. If you see the movies and the Ride of the Rohirim towards the pelenor fields doesn't move you emotionally, If don't feel any suspense at weathertop are not relieved at the first daylight of the fifth day then these movies are simply not for you and our tastes are not compatible. The more I think about it, I really do believe that LOTR is the Star Wars of my generation in terms of cultural significance.

It will be worth your time and will definitely leave a lasting impression on you as a viewer.It's my go to repeat films now and can watch it several times a week.
